title: The history of the games console
tagline: From a dot on an oscilloscope in 1958 to machines that trace rays of light sixty times a second.
intro: The first video games were built by physicists and students to show off laboratory machines. In 1972 a box that plugged into a television brought them home. Since then consoles have crashed, recovered, moved from cartridges to discs to downloads, and grown from a handful of logic chips into computers that paint millions of pixels every frame.

eras.name: Games in the laboratory
eras.summary: Scientists and students make games on oscilloscopes and room-sized computers. One engineer wonders whether a television could play them.

eras.name: The first consoles
eras.summary: Boxes for the television go on sale. Cartridges turn them into small computers. Then the American market collapses.

eras.name: Cartridges from Japan
eras.summary: Nintendo and Sega rebuild the business with better games, better controllers and 16-bit chips.

eras.name: Discs and 3D
eras.summary: Cheap optical discs and chips that draw polygons bring 3D worlds. Sony and then Microsoft join in.

eras.name: Online and high definition
eras.summary: Consoles connect to the internet, draw in high definition, and try new ways to play.

eras.name: Fast storage and ray tracing
eras.summary: Solid-state drives all but end loading screens. GPUs trace rays of light, and upscalers fill in pixels.

events.title: Tennis on an oscilloscope
events.where: Brookhaven National Laboratory, Upton, New York
events.text: For a visitors' day, physicist William Higinbotham wired an analog computer to a five-inch oscilloscope. Two people with a knob and a button each hit a glowing dot over a net. Hundreds of visitors queued to play Tennis for Two.
events.why: It is often called the first video game made purely for fun, though it was taken apart afterwards and forgotten for years.

events.title: Spacewar! spreads between computers
events.text: Students at MIT wrote a space duel for the new PDP-1 computer. Two ships circled a star and fired torpedoes. Copies passed from lab to lab wherever a PDP-1 stood.
events.why: It was the first video game played at many computer sites, and it inspired the first arcade machines.

events.title: The Brown Box plays games on a TV
events.who: Ralph Baer, Bill Harrison and Bill Rusch
events.text: Engineer Ralph Baer had the idea in August 1966: a box that lets an ordinary television play games. With two colleagues he built a series of prototypes. The seventh, wrapped in wood-grain tape, played ping-pong and target shooting.
events.why: This prototype, now in the Smithsonian, is the ancestor of every home console.

events.title: The first home console goes on sale
events.text: Magnavox sold Baer's design as the Odyssey for $99.95. It had no processor and no memory. It drew three square dots and a line, and players stuck plastic overlays on the TV screen for scenery. About 350,000 were sold.
events.why: Games had left the laboratory and entered the living room.

events.title: Pong comes home
events.text: Atari's arcade hit Pong, released on 29 November 1972, was squeezed onto a single chip for the home. Sears sold about 150,000 in the 1975 holiday season. Unlike the Odyssey, it kept score and made sound.
events.why: It showed that one custom chip could be a whole games machine, and it made consoles a mass product.

events.title: Games on swappable cartridges
events.who: Jerry Lawson's team at Fairchild; Wallace Kirschner and Lawrence Haskel at Alpex
events.text: The Fairchild Channel F was the first console built round a microprocessor and the first to take ROM cartridges. Jerry Lawson, one of the first Black engineers in the games industry, led the team that turned a prototype into a product.
events.why: From now on a console was a computer that ran whatever program you plugged in.

events.title: The Atari 2600
events.who: Atari (Jay Miner, Joe Decuir and others)
events.text: Atari's cartridge console cost $199 and had just 128 bytes of memory. Programmers had to build each line of the picture while the TV's beam was drawing it. It went on to sell about 30 million.
events.why: It made the console a fixture of the home, and Activision, founded in 1979, became the first company to make games for someone else's machine.

events.title: The great crash
events.text: Too many consoles and too many poor games flooded the shops. US home video game revenue fell from about $3.2 billion in 1983 to about $100 million in 1985. Atari buried unsold cartridges in a New Mexico landfill.
events.why: Many people decided consoles were a passing fad. Recovery came from Japan.

events.title: The Famicom
events.text: Nintendo's Family Computer went on sale in Japan for ¥14,800. Its controller used the flat cross-shaped D-pad that Gunpei Yokoi had designed for handheld games. Renamed the Nintendo Entertainment System, it was tested in New York from 18 October 1985.
events.why: It rebuilt the console business after the crash and sold 61.91 million.

events.title: 16 bits and a console war
events.text: Sega's Mega Drive, sold as the Genesis in North America from August 1989, used the 16-bit Motorola 68000 processor found in arcade machines. With Sonic the Hedgehog in 1991 it took on Nintendo head to head.
events.why: Rivalry between console makers became the engine of faster hardware.

events.title: A console in your pocket
events.who: Gunpei Yokoi and Satoru Okada, Nintendo
events.text: The Game Boy had a plain grey screen and modest parts, chosen on purpose so that four AA batteries would last for hours. Sold with Tetris, it reached 118.69 million units together with the Game Boy Color.
events.why: It proved that cheap, well-understood technology and a great game can beat more powerful rivals.

events.title: Nintendo walks away from Sony
events.text: Sony had been building a CD-ROM add-on for the Super Nintendo. At the Consumer Electronics Show in June 1991 it showed a machine called the Play Station. The next day, Nintendo announced it would work with Philips instead.
events.why: Sony engineer Ken Kutaragi persuaded his company to build its own console.

events.title: The PlayStation
events.who: Ken Kutaragi's team at Sony Computer Entertainment
events.text: Sony's console went on sale in Japan for ¥39,800. It was built to draw 3D worlds out of flat polygons, and its games came on cheap CDs rather than costly cartridges. It reached North America on 9 September 1995.
events.why: It became the first console to ship more than 100 million units, and it made 3D the normal way to play.

events.title: A thumb stick as standard
events.text: The Nintendo 64's controller had an analog stick in the middle, so players could steer through 3D space by degrees. Super Mario 64 showed how. The console kept cartridges, which loaded fast but held little.
events.why: Analog sticks became part of every controller that followed.

events.title: Controllers start to shake
events.text: Nintendo's Rumble Pak, sold in Japan from 27 April 1997, shook the controller with a small motor. On 20 November 1997 Sony launched the DualShock, with two analog sticks and two motors of different sizes in its handles.
events.why: Two sticks and built-in vibration became the standard layout of a gamepad.

events.title: A console with a modem
events.text: Sega's Dreamcast came with a modem for playing over a telephone line. Phantasy Star Online let console players adventure together across countries. But sales reached only 9.13 million, and in 2001 Sega stopped making consoles.
events.why: It was early proof that consoles would go online.

events.title: The PlayStation 2
events.text: The PS2 played DVD films as well as games, at a time when DVD players were expensive. Many families bought one for both. It stayed in production until January 2013.
events.why: With more than 160 million sold by Sony's count, it is the best-selling console so far.

events.title: Microsoft builds a console
events.who: Seamus Blackley, Kevin Bachus, Ted Hase and Otto Berkes, Microsoft
events.text: The Xbox was close to a PC inside: a Pentium III processor, an Nvidia graphics chip and an 8 GB hard disk, the first built into a console. It also had a network socket. Xbox Live, its online service, opened on 15 November 2002.
events.why: Hard disks, PC parts and a built-in online service became the pattern for later consoles.

events.title: High definition, and a lesson in heat
events.text: The Xbox 360 brought high-definition pictures and wireless controllers as standard. But many consoles failed, showing three red lights. In July 2007 Microsoft extended the warranty to three years and set aside more than $1 billion for repairs.
events.why: It showed how hard it is to keep powerful chips cool in a small box.

events.title: The PlayStation 3 and the Cell
events.text: The PS3 used the Cell, an unusual processor with one main core and several helper cores, and it played Blu-ray discs. It was powerful but hard to program. In 2010 the US Air Force Research Laboratory linked 1,760 PS3s into a supercomputer.
events.why: Its difficulties pushed Sony towards ordinary PC-style chips next time.

events.title: The Wii gets everyone moving
events.who: Satoru Iwata, Shigeru Miyamoto and Genyo Takeda, Nintendo
events.text: Nintendo's Wii was much less powerful than its rivals. Instead it had a remote with an accelerometer and an infrared pointer, so players swung it like a racket. It sold 101.63 million.
events.why: It showed that a new way to play can matter more than faster chips.

events.title: The PlayStation 4
events.who: Mark Cerny, lead system architect, Sony
events.text: The PS4 used an 8-core AMD processor of the same family as a PC's, with 8 GB of memory shared between the CPU and the graphics. Games were stored on a 5,400 rpm hard disk. It sold more than 117 million.
events.why: Consoles became tuned, tightly packed PCs, which made games much easier to develop.

events.title: The Switch: home console and handheld
events.text: The Nintendo Switch is a tablet built round a mobile chip. It plays on its own screen, or slots into a dock to play on a TV. By 30 June 2026 Nintendo had sold 156.59 million.
events.why: It became Nintendo's best-selling console, second only to the PlayStation 2 by the makers' own counts.

events.title: The Road to PS5
events.text: In a technical talk, Mark Cerny set out the PlayStation 5's design: an 8-core Zen 2 processor, a ray-tracing GPU, and a custom SSD reading 5.5 GB a second, about a hundred times faster than the PS4's hard disk.
events.why: It moved fast storage from a nice extra to the centre of console design.

events.title: The PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X
events.text: Microsoft's Xbox Series X and S arrived on 10 November 2020 and Sony's PlayStation 5 on 12 November in the first countries. Both use 8-core AMD Zen 2 processors, ray-tracing graphics and fast SSDs. The PS5's controller added voice-coil haptics and triggers that push back.
events.why: Loading screens shrank from half a minute to a few seconds.

events.title: The PS5 reaches India
events.text: After a wait of almost three months, the PlayStation 5 went on sale in India at Rs 49,990, with the Digital Edition listed at Rs 39,990. Pre-orders had opened on 12 January.
events.why: A worldwide chip shortage meant consoles stayed hard to buy for many months, in India and everywhere else.

events.title: Why sticks drift
events.text: Repair specialists at iFixit took apart the PS5's controller. Its thumb sticks use potentiometers rated for 2 million cycles, which heavy players can reach in a few hundred hours. Wear on the carbon track is one main cause of stick drift.
events.why: It explained a fault that affects controllers from every maker, and renewed interest in magnetic Hall-effect sticks.

events.title: A console that upscales with machine learning
events.text: The PlayStation 5 Pro has a GPU about 45% faster than the PS5's. It also has PSSR, an upscaler that uses a trained neural network to turn a lower-resolution picture into a sharp 4K one.
events.why: Drawing fewer pixels and filling in the rest cleverly is now a main route to better pictures.

events.title: The Switch 2
events.text: Nintendo's successor to the Switch kept the hybrid idea and ran most Switch games. Nintendo reported 23.68 million sold by 30 June 2026.
events.why: The handheld-and-TV console is now a lasting form, not a one-off.

facts: The first home console, the Magnavox Odyssey, had no processor and no memory. It could draw three square dots and one line.
The Atari 2600 had 128 bytes of memory. A PlayStation 5 has 16 gigabytes: over a hundred million times more.
In 2010 the US Air Force Research Laboratory built a supercomputer out of 1,760 PlayStation 3 consoles.
The PlayStation exists because a deal between Sony and Nintendo fell apart at a trade show in June 1991.
A PlayStation 5's SSD can read in one second what a PlayStation 4's hard disk needed about a minute to read.
